clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant disorder from germline ETV6 mutations causing mild-to-moderate thrombocytopenia with normal-sized platelets
Bleeding is generally mild but the platelets often show a functional defect contributing to symptoms
There is a predisposition to haematological malignancy, notably B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia in childhood as well as myeloid neoplasms
Unlike RUNX1 and ANKRD26 disorders, the leukaemia spectrum prominently includes lymphoid as well as myeloid malignancy
A family history spanning thrombocytopenia and childhood leukaemia is an important clue
Some carriers also show mild red-cell macrocytosis or other subtle blood-count changes
Diagnosis relies on germline ETV6 sequencing, ideally confirmed on non-haematopoietic tissue
Relatives considered as stem-cell donors must be screened for the familial variant
reference.pathophysiology: ETV6 encodes an ETS-family transcriptional repressor essential for haematopoietic stem-cell function and megakaryocyte development. Germline mutations, often affecting the DNA-binding domain, act in a dominant-negative fashion and mislocalise the protein, impairing normal transcriptional repression and disturbing megakaryopoiesis to reduce platelet output. The same disruption of a key haematopoietic regulator destabilises lymphoid and myeloid progenitors, so affected individuals carry a heightened risk of acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and myeloid neoplasms once additional somatic changes accumulate.
additionalDifferentials: RUNX1 familial platelet disorder with myeloid malignancy
Familial acute lymphoblastic leukaemia from other predisposition genes (for example PAX5)
Other inherited thrombocytopenias with normal platelet size
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count with film review for platelet size and red-cell indices
Germline ETV6 sequencing on a non-haematopoietic source such as fibroblasts
Platelet function testing where bleeding is disproportionate
Bone marrow examination with cytogenetics at baseline and for surveillance
Periodic monitoring of the blood count for evolving cytopenias or blasts
Screening of potential related stem-cell donors for the familial mutation
redFlags: New lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, bone pain, or circulating blasts suggesting acute leukaemia
Progressive or additional cytopenias on surveillance
Emergence of a clonal cytogenetic or molecular abnormality
Constitutional symptoms such as fever, weight loss, or night sweats
reference.prognosis: The thrombocytopenia itself is usually mild, but the disorder carries a meaningful lifetime risk of leukaemia, particularly childhood acute lymphoblastic leukaemia; prognosis depends on early recognition of malignant transformation and on the outcome of leukaemia-directed treatment.
pitfalls: Attributing the low count to immune thrombocytopenia and giving unnecessary immunosuppression
Failing to recognise the lymphoid (not only myeloid) leukaemia predisposition
Testing only peripheral blood DNA when a clone may obscure the germline variant
Neglecting germline screening of related potential transplant donors
references: Nathan and Oski's Hematology and Oncology of Infancy and Childhood
management: Recognise that the mild-to-moderate thrombocytopenia usually needs no routine treatment, reserving platelet transfusion or antifibrinolytics for significant bleeding or surgical cover
Avoid antiplatelet drugs and provide bleeding precautions given the associated platelet functional defect
Lifelong haematological surveillance with periodic blood counts and bone marrow examination for evolving cytopenias, dysplasia or blasts
Prompt leukaemia-directed treatment if B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia or a myeloid neoplasm develops
Autosomal dominant genetic counselling with germline ETV6 testing on a non-haematopoietic source such as fibroblasts
Screen potential related stem-cell donors for the familial ETV6 mutation before transplantation
